speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
When this question was reached,
Wheat Marketing

Mr. Speaker, during the calling of questions, I requested the house to be good enough to permit the matter to stand until the orders of the day were called so that I might make a short statement. The questions are:
1.	Has the government directly or indirectly purchased grain in the Winnipeg or any other hi a t k e t ?
2.	If so, what is the cost of the grain so purchased?
3.	Under what statutory authority were such purchases made?
These questions were asked in the first instance before the orders of the day were called; subsequently they were treated as notices, and the questions appeared on the order paper to-day. In 1930 representations were made to the government that it should fix a price for wheat and become responsible for the payment of that price. I think the figure mentioned was 70 cents per bushel. The government declined to entertain the proposal suggested, and no action of that character was taken.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: May I inquire who made the request?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: The pools, the provinces and others.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: To the present government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Yes; it was subsequent
to August 7, after the present administration came into power. As a matter of fact it was subsequent to the development of the difficulties experienced by the pools in connection with the guarantees given by the provinces, that resulted in some adjustments being made. Late in the fall of that year Mr. John I. McFarland became general manager of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, which was not a cooperative agency in the western provinces but the selling agency for the pools operating in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. He was appointed to that position; he accepted the appointment without salary, and he is still discharging the duties of that office.
It will be recalled that last year we paid a bonus of five cents a bushel on wheat produced in western Canada. That action was subject to some criticism; recently one of the farm organizations in Manitoba passed a resolution against the continuance of that policy, and some members of the House of Commons from Alberta have made fairly strong speeches in opposition to it. The other day I indicated that financial conditions did not warrant the continuance of that bonus.

In order that hon. members may have a general view of the situation I would ask them to permit me to point out that we have a very large country elevator storage in western Canada. We have five internal elevators for storage purposes at Lethbridge, Calgary, Edmonton, Saskatoon and Moose Jaw, and we have, of course, large storage facilities east of the great lakes. The storage at the head of the lakes approximates 93,000,000 bushels, and the storage east of the lakes approximates 75,500,000, and west of the lakes, including country elevators, the capacity is something like 223,000,000 bushels. So far as licensed elevators are concerned, we have thus over 390,000,000 bushels storage capacity. There is unlicensed capacity to the extent of about 25,000,000 bushels.
In the ordinary course, wheat produced by the farmer is hauled to the country elevator point. He then determines whether or not he will sell it or accept a storage ticket for it. This house is, of course, familiar with the machinery provided by the Grain Act for dealing with matters of this kind. If he accepts his storage ticket his grain is then in the elevator and it is carried by the elevator company under the conditions set out in the Grain Act. He might, of course, sell it at any time on the strength of the certificate thus issued, which indicates the number of bushels of grain he has, in a broad general way its grade, and whether or not it is under special bin or ordinary bin storage. But in some cases, I think it is fair to say, the farmer sells his grain outright to the elevator company, or whoever may be the purchaser at the moment; and in some instances, of course, the farmer, under the act, ships his grain over the loading platform into the car, if he has a carload, which he himself may forward to Fort William or elsewhere as he may be advised.
Bearing that fact in mind, I would point out that this year we have a very large crop. The figures I have received up to date would indicate that 225,000,000 bushels of this year's crop have left the farmers' fields and been unloaded at the country elevators throughout western Canada. It is difficult to say, but it is quite clear that a substantial part of that has been sold from these elevators. The figures I have would indicate that out of that approximately 225,000,000 bushels now delivered 175,000,000 bushels have actually been sold, which would mean that more than 50 per cent of this year's crop has actually been sold out of the hands of the farmers and elevators and grain dealers into the hands of

Wheat Marketing
those who ultimately receive it. Last year the entire crop, so far as we have a record -and we have, perhaps, a closer record of last year's than of most years, because of the bonus paid-the total crop sold by the farmers amounted to 265,000,000 bushels. That is to say, they marketed that quantity. This year it will thus be observed that, the crop being much larger, we have already marketed 225,000,000 bushels or within 40,000,000 bushels of last year's. The amazing thing in this year's movement is that over the period beginning in 1922, to date, for the three months of August, September and October, we have actually exported more wheat out of this country in those three months than in that period since 1922 but one year. That is, it amounts to approximately 120,000,000 bushels, notwithstanding the very low price that has been paid for it.
Having directed the attention of the house to the crop and the manner in which it is disposed of, I shall now endeavour, very briefly for the sake of some of my eastern colleagues of this House of Commons, to point out the manner in which it is financed. The elevator companies have a substantial operating capital. When the farmer brings his grain into the elevator, desiring to dispose of it for cash, the elevator company issue him a cheque and the grain then becomes their property. Obviously, the elevator company do not have working capital sufficient to enable them to purchase outright all the wheat offered, so they secure through the banks the necessary advances to enable them, with their working capital, to carry on the purchase of wheat offered. It may be said that if the elevator companies have a working capital, of 25 to 30 per cent, that is all that might be necessary, for the banks are willing to advance, on the security of hypothecated grain, the remaining 70 or 75 per cent of the purchase price; and, of course, the grain being insured, held in storage and hypothecated to the bank, the bank holds a security for its 70 or 75 per cent-it may be less-of the total purchase price, the promise to pay of the purchaser, being the elevator company, being usually in the form of a promissory note. These adjustments are made, of course, at the end of each day as the grain comes into the country elevator point. The banks insist that, as the money is the money of their depositors, they should be protected against possible fluctuations in the market- and market fluctuations have been, of course, very marked during the last few years. The technical term used is that the transaction shall be hedged, which merely means that
somewhere there should be somebody prepared to buy an option on wheat that has been sold; in other words, that there should be no such violent fluctuations of the market, between the date of purchase and the dates fixed in the hedging operation, as would imperil in any sense the security of the bank, or render possible any loss being made.
The purchase of futures, as it is called in this hedging operation, has heretofore in this country been carried on by two classes, speaking broadly: (a) the investor; and (b) the speculator. In the first class were the milling companies or the purchasers abroad, what we will call those engaged in the grain business, who purchase wheat as a commodity in their line of business and deal with it as an investment for the purposes of their business. These operations continue to some extent, of course, curtailed naturally by the recent diminution in trade throughout the world. The second class, the speculator, has practically disappeared. There has been some speculation in Canada in wheat during the last six or eight months, the buying having been from Chicago; but I think I am correct in saying that, broadly, the speculator is no longer in evidence as a purchaser of wheat. Therefore, so far as hedging operations are concerned, you have the disappearance of the speculator, who thereby played a very important part, as Sir Josiah Stamp pointed out in his report, in connection with the marketing of wheat; and you have left the investor, with his ability to purchase curtailed by reason of the general trade depression.
Under these circumstances, Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, to which I have referred, became the only available hedging organization left in western Canada, and the government is faced at the moment with the issue as to whether or not, under these circumstances, it would give its support as provided by the Relief Act passed in 1931 and 1932 as well-this being a product of the field and the farm-by guaranteeing to the banks such sums as might be necessary to enable these operations to be carried on by this organization. But before that was done the government had to consider whether or not the interest of Canada as a whole would be best served by continuing the bonus which we granted last year or by taking the steps I have just indicated for the purpose of protecting the general situation in connection with the marketing of wheat,
I need hardly say to the house that it gave us very great anxiety and concern, but it was quite apparent from the reports we received from every person interested in the trade
Wheat Marketing

that unless hedging operations could be carried on there could be no marketing of this year's crop. The result would be that the price of wheat would fall back to less than forty cents per bushel. Therefore, not pegging the price and not interfering in any sense with the operations of the law of supply and demand but to secure the orderly and regulated disposition of the crop, the steps I have indicated were taken and the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Pools, Limited became the hedging agency in order to enable, with the assistance of the government, sales to take place and the crop to be marketed. As I have indicated, there has been marketed at the moment at least 175,000,000 bushels of the crop of this year and there has been delivered to the elevators up to Saturday roughly 225,000,000 bushels of this year's crop. While the price has fallen, it has fallen in an orderly manner and in accordance with the increased supply which, as I mentioned the other day, is out of all proportion to the demand. The crop in the southern hemisphere is now available which augments the supply by another 250,000,000 bushels. This will be in addition to the very large crop of our own country and the tremendous carryover in the United States, now in the hands of the farm board, and the relatively small carry-over in this country.
I hasten to assure the house that on a balance of financial benefits it is clear that in respect of any obligations which might be incurred-it is not possible that any heavy obligations will be incurred unless something very unforeseen happens-the amount involved will be less than would be involved by the payment of the bonus requested. Weighing the situation as a whole, the probabilities pro and con, the effect upon the dominion, the business which would be secured and the chaos which would result from the absolute failure to sell wheat except as a distress commodity, the steps which I have indicated were taken.
If I might say so, I do not think any good purpose would be served by going into the details of the operations which we have entrusted to the organizations I have mentioned under the management of Mr. McFarland. However, the closest supervision has been exercised and we believe and we have had no reason to change our minds at the present moment, that the steps taken will be more beneficial to the dominion as a whole and will secure for the country as a whole greater advantages than if we paid the producer the bonus which was paid last year and which we are pressed to continue this year.

Except for the mention of the exact financial amount involved, which obviously it is difficult to give, I think I have answered all the questions asked not only by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) but also by one other hon. gentleman sitting to his left who asked a similar question some days ago.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
To the banks. The
banks have advanced the sum of money necessary to enable the operations to be carried on and this has been done on the strength of the security of the options and of our guarantee. Any possible loss would occur through the proceeds of the sales of the commodity not being sufficient to pay the obligations.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Would they not have recourse first to the pools who are the original debtors?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
This is not a pool, it is
a selling agency.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Selling agency for the pool?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: It is merely an organization backed up by our guarantee to carry on hedging operations to enable the grain to be sold in this country.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
They have no capital of
their own?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
It is not that sort of an
organization; it is a selling organization.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: If there is any loss, the government will sustain it?

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Am I right in understanding that this guarantee is given under the Unemployment Relief Act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
I believe the correct
name is the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Has anything of this character been done with last year's crop or is it just in connection with this year's crop?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: It has been done with respect to last year's crop. Since 1930 when it was taken over this organization has permitted the possible marketing in this country of Canadian wheat.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Will the Prime
Minister be good enough to explain the present position of the durum wheat growers in Manitoba who delivered their crop to the 1930-31 pool which Mr. McFarland took over? There are about a thousand of these men who have been treated rather unfairly and I was wondering if the Prime Minister had an explanation to offer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows as well as anyone that that is not a
matter with which the selling agency had to do. The Manitoba wheat pool purchased the durum wheat and under the provisions of their contract there was to be an adjustment so that the seller would receive what had been stipulated in the contract. Unfortunately this organization, which is not the one Mr. McFarland controls, has not been able to make any such adjustments.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
The point is
that Mr. McFarland took that wheat over and was responsible for the ultimate selling of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. McFarland was
accountable to the Manitoba wheat pool to which he did account. The contract was between the Manitoba wheat pool and the growers themselves and no one else. I trust the hon. gentleman will realize that there is no contract between the selling agency which Mr. McFarland manages, and the growers. He had no relations with them, contractual or otherwise. Any grain he received was, like the wheat he received, from the Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta wheat pool. He received that for sale and dealt with them on that basis.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: If I understand aright what the Prime Minister said, if there is a loss in this hedging operation of the selling agency of Mr. McFarland, then the banks make up the loss and the government makes up that loss to the banks. But on the other side, supposing there is a profit, do the banks, or does Mr. McFarland as a selling agent, or does the government take the profit? How does the Prime Minister think this arrangement will assist the seventy municipalities that had no crop whatever this year and will have to buy their seed for next year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker,
you have been very generous in extending the widest possible latitude in regard to questions; but when you get into that of relief to municipalities, you are far away from the question under consideration. The advances made by the banks are guaranteed by the country and if, after payment of the advances, a profit remains, it belongs to the agency and not to the government.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
I should like to ask
the Prime Minister a question based on the reply which he gave to the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir): Is he telling us now that John I. McFarland was in the employ partly of the government and also of the Manitoba pool sales agency?
Wheat Marketing

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
He said nothing of the
sort. Why should the hon. gentleman endeavour to mislead? If he had followed me, he certainly could not have made that statement. Mr. McFarland is receiving no salary from anyone. The most experienced grain man on this continent once told me he believed Mr. McFarland was the best grain man in North America. Whether he was right is a matter of individual opinion. Mr. McFarland was not appointed by this government. He was appointed to his position, not by the Manitoba pool but by the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, and the appointment, needless to say, was warmly approved by the government. He has been carrying on since on that basis.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: As the right hon. gentleman has said that it would serve no good purpose to give any more details about the situation and as the explanations that he has already given are most interesting, would he have any objection to having the galleries cleared in order that he may give full information to the house? I have asked the Prime Minister for an answer.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: No.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the
government to permit this transaction to be carried on indefinitely, or is there an understanding as to the probable date when it will be terminated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
No one knows better
than does the hon. member for Weyburn the difficulty of answering that question. Obviously he knows you could not say that you would do it on this date or that, but it will be done because you must consider the market situation from the standpoint of the producer. If it were desired to wreck the market, that could be done. If it be desired in an orderly or regular manner to dispose of the crop, that cannot be done until such time as the absorbing power of the market enables the transaction to be completed without stress.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Referring to the matter
of advances, mentioned this afternoon, has an order in council been passed covering this question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
I think the matter was
covered by letters to the banks. That is my memory of it. There may be an order in council. I will look it up and let the hon. gentleman know. But there were orders in council with respect to all the assistance given by the government to the Alberta, Saskat-

chewan and Manitoba pools, and the orders in council last year were tabled just as the orders in council this year have been tabled. No liability has arisen under any of these orders in council nor is there likely to be any so far as I know, but owing to conditions of which this house has full knowledge it was thought to be in the national interest that the situation should be clarified to enable the working capital of the pools to permit them carrying on their operations without question, and the guarantees were given to them, and I think copies of all the orders in council have been laid on the table of the house.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Copies of these orders in council have been tabled?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: So far as the three pools were concerned.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: But I mean this year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
As to the selling agency
order in council, I am not sure. There were letters written covering the situation. They may or may not have been reduced to orders in council. I will ascertain and let the hon. gentleman know.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Surely the government
cannot act in any other way than by order in council. The statute requires it. Under the Relief Measures Act passed last year the governor in council acts, not by means of letters and correspondence; but the statute requires that every one of these orders and regulations shall be tabled forthwith in the house, and when parliament is not in session that they shall be published in the official gazette. I would like to know whether this will be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
There was no necessity
for an order in council until such time as the transaction was reduced to a position where an order in council could speak with certainty. That is, at the moment the banks make such advances as may be necessary on the strength of the assurance of the government that at the appropriate time when the liability is determined the order in council will be passed, which, as the hon. gentleman will realize, is the ordinary course in matters of this kind because the amount has not been determined. As soon as it is, necessarily the order in council will be passed.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
May I ask
if this has been the policy since 1930, of continuously hedging all the grain handled by the selling agency without any check up?

Wheat Marketing

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Oh no, the matter has
been checked.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
What was
the amount of the loss last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asks, what was the loss last year? As a matter of fact, on one day when I was speaking in this house there was a profit.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
On one
day?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: On several days.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
The Prime
Minister knows perfectly well that the market has been dropping for the last two years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman says that I know that perfectly well, there was what you call a blackboard loss when Mr. McFarland was appointed with our acquiescence. He knows as well as any other man in the world what the position of the pools was with respect to Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. He knows exactly what loss was involved in Saskatchewan, and he knows what the effect of it was on the fortunes of the pools both there and in Manitoba. In Alberta the situation was much more favourable. The hon. gentleman also knows that there were, not days, but many times when the selling operation would have resulted in a profit.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
I am not
referring to that at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
I am answering the
question.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
As a matter of profit and
loss?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Purely. So far as this
particular moment is concerned, undoubtedly there will be a loss, but whether or not in the final determination of the matter there is a loss will depend entirely, as I mentioned to the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) on circumstances about which I do not venture to express an opinion.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
There is one point I would
like to bring out in connection with the guarantee. I have been listening closely and I understand that the government is guaranteeing only to the banks and that the banks are financing only 75 per cent. There is no guarantee to the elevator man. The government is simply looking after the banks?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman, I
am sorry to say, has confused two things. The question of the purchase by the elevators has nothing to do with it at all in any way,
shape or form. We were dealing with the selling agency as such and with the hedging, without which the sale of grain in this country was practically an impossibility.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
I would like to draw the attention of the government to a despatch from Manitoba, because this places the matter before the Prime Minister and the government just as it appears to the ordinary individual in Manitoba. It says:
During the winter of 1930-31 the federal government took over the grain then held by the Canadian pools and placed Mr. John I. McFarland in control. This grain has not yet been all disposed of, many millions of bushels still remaining unsold. The grain still on hand is all spring wheat, all the durum having been sold and cleared out early in the spring of 1931. To the credit of the durum growers who pooled their wheat from the 1930 crop there remains about $450,000. which should have been paid to them early in the summer of 1931.
What the durum growers want to know is why this amount is not being paid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
There could be perhaps, Mr. Speaker, more misstatements in a few lines than in the passage which the hon. gentleman has quoted, but I can hardly conceive it possible. First of all, the government did not place Mr. McFarland in charge. The directors of the organization elected him to that position. That is number one.
Number two is that there was no contact between the organization and the durum wheat growers. They did their business with the Manitoba pool, and to that pool they should look for redress. I happen to have met a delegation of them here a year ago. I went into their papers and went over their matter fully, and I think satisfied them abundantly that whatever right they had was against the Manitoba pool, and that with respect to the selling agency nothing could be done. That was an organization that had no contract, and still further, no contact, with them. It was quite clear to me that the selling agency did receive durum wheat as well as other wheat for sale, and did sell it and account for it. These matters are audited every week, and they accounted for it. So far as the durum growers having any relation to the government or to the organization of which Mr. McFarland is general manager is concerned, it was abundantly clear to me, and they had to admit it, that they had not any. Their contract was with the Manitoba pool, and to that pool, being the other party to the contract, they must look.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
May I ask one other question for my own information? Apart entirely
109S
Wheat Marketing

from the guarantees to the banks in regard to hedging operations, is the government making actual cash advances on this year's crop to the pool?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
No. I tried to explain
to the house that there are three pools, in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and the pools have working capital which is ample up to the present to carry on their operations, but in seeking credit with the banks, owing to the position of the province with which they were formerly identified, they sought assistance from us, the same assistance as we gave last year without incurring any liability, and after the closest investigation of the situation we saw no likelihood, and see none now, of any obligation or liability of any kind being incurred, and wre passed the same order in council to meet the situation, a copy of which I am quite certain has been laid on the table.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
In regard to the pools this
year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
Yes, but no money has
been advanced and I cannot see any possibility or likelihood of it.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
What would be the use of
it if there was no chance of a liability?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext:
I will tell you why. The
pools got into difficulty and they had to give certain securities to the province to make good the liabilities which they incurred to the province. In order that their working capital might be protected for this purpose, the banks sought some further security to enable them to establish their credits, without any question of it being interfered with, and we acted in that sense.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: The Prime Minister just made a statement to the effect that there would be a certain amount of probable loss in connection with the marketing of the western wheat crop.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: He did not say that at all.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Is that the reason the government has refused to give a bushel or acreage bonus to the western farmers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the 'hon. gentleman had been good enough to follow my observations he must realize that his question was answered before he asked it.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Perhaps you might answer it again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: I think I am under no obligation to answer it again, no obligation whatever.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Well, amplify it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: It was amplified to such an extent that I thought I was saying more than I should. There was no necessity of going to the extent to which I did. I tried to explain to the hon. gentleman that in balancing what we considered to be advantages and disadvantages we concluded that we could best serve the interests of the dominion as a whole, including the farmers of western Canada, by taking the action we did take, namely that of securing the possibility of there being some organization which provided hedging. Otherwise the whole business of the marketing of grain would have been in chaos, and there would have been a debacle on a scale, which if the hon. gentleman desires to understand fully, he need only ask those who are interested in the disposition of grain in this country.

maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope the Prime Minister will permit me one question; I realize he has been long suffering. See if I understand him correctly: The wheat bonus is to be discontinued this year, but in lieu of that the farmers are to be assisted through the medium of this government guaranteeing the banks against any loss in their business relations with the Wheat Producers Limited, or other farm organization? To repeat, is it a fact that there is to be no wheat bonus this year, but in lieu of that the farmers are to be assisted by this government guaranteeing the banks?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT MARKETING
subtopic: GOVERNMENT GUARANTEE OF ADVANCES BY BANKS TO SELLING AGENCY
speechtext: That is not what was said, and I am sure the hon. member for Melville must realize that he has hardly made an adequate summary of what has been said. I shall endeavour to put it charitably and state simply he has not summarized the situation correctly. I have no doubt if he carefully analyzes what I save said he will realize what the position was and what action was taken. It does not seem possible to me that my words are capable of just the construction he has placed upon them.

maintopic: WHEAT SHIPMENTS
WHEAT SHIPMENTS
subtopic: INTERPRETATION OF PROVISIONS OF BRITISH IMPORTS DUTIES ACT, 1932

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: WHEAT SHIPMENTS
subtopic: INTERPRETATION OF PROVISIONS OF BRITISH IMPORTS DUTIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I desire to ask the Prime Minister a couple of questions based upon a Canadian Press despatch appearing in maritime newspapers of this morning, November 14. The despatch reads:

Ukrainian Minority in Poland
Wheat Preference
Ottawa, Nov.	13.-Grain	exporters in
Winnipeg do not anticipate any difficulty in shipments of Canadian wheat through United States to the United Kingdom obtaining six cents a bushel preference, it was declared in government circles here tonight. Some changes would have to be made in the methods of shipments and in some cases there might be delay required to -prove that it was Canadian wheat when it reached the United Kingdom ports but the dealers were not expecting -any important obstacles in routing through the United States.
Last week in the House of Commons the question of whether Canadian wheat held in United States elevators on its way to Britain would get the benefit of the preference. It was claimed by some speakers that wheat stored in United States elevators could not later be identified as Canadian wheat and therefore could not get a preference.
Of course a great deal of wheat going from Canada through United States ports is consigned to other European countries and the preference would have no bearing on such shipments.
As this despatch seems to 'be in conflict with the statements ma-de by the Prime Minister on November 10, 1932, as found on page 1045 of Hansard, referring to statutory conditions of British regulation number 12, as follows:
(b) Consignment to the United Kingdom on a through transit-if I might use that word

although the transit might be interrupted; but as long as the point of origin is fixed and the destination is the United Kingdom, even though there were delays in the transit the preference applies.
I should like to ask this question:
(1)	Will the Prime Minister state to the house what he meant by "delays" and "interruption in ' transit" as stated by him on November 10?
(2)	Will Canadian wheat in transit stored in elevators located in the United States enjoy the six cent preference?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: WHEAT SHIPMENTS
subtopic: INTERPRETATION OF PROVISIONS OF BRITISH IMPORTS DUTIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The hon. senior member for Halifax sent me a copy of the memorandum which he has just read. I do not think I can add anything to what has already been said and which appears many times in the pages of Hansard. I think the regulation under which the British government operates has been set out in Hansard at least three times. The conditions under which grain destined for the United Kingdom will receive the preference when it is not shipped direct to that country were, first, that it should be of empire origin-and when I say grain, it should be in this instance of Canadian origin-second, that it should be consigned to the United Kingdom; and third, it would then be entitled to receive the preference if it were conveyed there even although it were interrupted in
course of transit. I tried to make it abundantly clear that the regulations which deal with commodities generally and not only with grain, and have reference not to the United States alone but to other countries as well, contemplate goods which are of empire origin being conveyed to the United Kingdom through other than wholly British territory. In the case of the United States grain may be held in bond for a period of six months without paying duty. After it has been in bond for that time, it becomes dutiable by the United States at the rate of forty-two cents a bushel. When it is received in bond in the United States, if it is consigned to the United Kingdom, although the transit were delayed and there is an interruption in the directness of the transit, the regulation that I read the other day made it abundantly clear that such a commodity was entitled to the preference. The action taken by the various members of the House of Commons, of course, was not the action of the British government, and this government would find it extremely difficult to take any course apart from those which exist under well

established practices in diplomacy. I think the hon. gentleman would be the first to realize the character of the difficulties which would have to be overcome before the government could support the action taken by non-official members of the British House of Commons.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the Customs Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton South) in the chair.
On section 1-Valuation of imports.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I assume that this section is intended to implement in part article 16 of the trade agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not think that is specifically referred to. This was requested by the British delegation, as well as by the representatives of other parts of the empire, and we agreed to submit it to parliament.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Let me read article 16:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that customs administration in Canada shall be governed by such general principles as will ensure (a) the avoidance, so far as reasonably possible, of uncertainty as to the amount of customs duties and other fiscal imposts payable on the arrival of goods in Canada; (b) the reduction of delay and friction to a minimum; and (c) the provision of machinery for the prompt and impartial settlement of disputes in matters appertaining to the application of tariffs.
On reading this bill I gathered that it was an endeavour on the part of the Canadian government to carry out at least part of that article.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I would say to my right hon. friend that this amendment was independent of that article. As a matter of fact it was agreed to before that agreement was signed. It was thought by the representatives of the United Kingdom that it would be in the interests of Great Britain if this section in the act did not apply to United Kingdom exports, and after consideration and deliberation it was agreed to as a consideration by us to them, for which they asked and to which we agreed.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would ask that the discussion be carried on in a little louder tone of voice. So far we have been unable to hear what has been said by the leader of the opposition and the minister.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Is the minister saying that this bill now before us is not in any way related to the Canada-United Kingdom trade agreement, but is something altogether apart from it?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: This was part of the general agreements which have been expressed in the United Kingdom agreement now before the house. This amendment implements another agreement made with the representatives of the United Kingdom.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the minister should thank me for having helped him give a correct interpretation, because his first statement appears now to have been quite wrong.
Customs Act

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am always glad to offer thanks when they are due.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Now may I ask if this particular amendment is going to serve the interests of Canada. I assume for the moment that it is restricted to trade between Great Britain and Canada. Why should it not be made applicable to trade generally? If the principle is sound why should it not be applied generally?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I hope my right hon. frend will pardon me if I point out that his party was instrumental in putting upon the statute books legislation which created a British preference. I can think of many cases under that preference where, in the interests of trade, articles reached Canada free of duty from the United Kingdom while they were charged from 20 per cent to 35 per cent under the intermediate and general tariffs. It is thought to be in the general interest to bring about this amendment. If my right hon. friend should ask I would say that if we had not been requested to surrender this right with regard to Great Britain, it would not have been surrendered. I think it was a good thing when it was brought in; I think it has helped the country. It may be that we will suffer in some degree, but the loss that is occasioned on the left will be made lip by the profit on the right.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then, from what my hon. friend has said, we have to thank Great Britain rather than our own government for bringing about this change, which will be advantageous not only to Great Britain but to Canada as well. I think it is a step in the right direction; I think on behalf of the Canadian people we owe an obligation to the British government for having influenced our own administration to this extent. The minister looks upon it only from the point of view of what it means to Great Britain. I am inclined to view it in the light of what it will mean to the great body of consumers and importers in Canada,

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In our tariff legislation we have given Great Britain a preference; in many cases her goods enter free while similar goods from other countries are taxed heavily. This is along the same line; it is giving something to Great Britain.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Whatever may have been the motive behind the introduction of this amendment I think I can safely say that the government are to be congratulated on taking a step in the right direction, unless my interpretation of the section is incorrect. I rise for 
the purpose of confirming my idea of what this amendment means. I take it that the introduction of this clause means that the power given the Minister of National Revenue, under the amendment of 1930, to place fixed valuations to any amount upon any commodities imported into Canada, is now removed with regard to goods coming under the British preference. Am I correct in that understanding?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think in substance the hon. member is correct, but his statement is not quite right. For instance, the minister has not that power; the governor general Tn council authorizes the minister to fix a valuation, upon his report.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am afraid that is a bit
of quibbling-I do not mean to be offensive.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
With regard to the
working of this section, the governor general, on the report of the minister, authorizes him to fix a value, and I submit that that has been most helpful to the business of this country. I am glad that it remains with respect to other countries, in just the same way as I am glad that our tariff, intermediate and general, remains where we give it free to Great Britain.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend sees criticism where there is none. I am merely trying to establish in my own mind, and for the benefit of other members as well, exactly what is the significance of this, and I am asking this question. Does it not mean that the power which was given to the government to fix values on all commodities imported into Canada, by giving that power to the Minister of National Revenue, has been removed so far as goods coming under the British preference are concerned?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes, or lower.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Or lower, yes; I was going
to comment on that also. It means, therefore, that there can be no longer any dump imposed on goods coming from Great Britain under the British preference. Am I correct?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
So far as goods are
concerned, under this section.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I would ask the minister
why that particular phrase is included "or any lower tariff." Are we likely to have tariffs lower to other countries than to Great Britain?

Customs Act

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: We have now in certain cases tariffs lower than against Great Britain. For instance, under the Australian trade agreement, meats come in-there is quite a large number of items, cheese, as I remember, being among them-at a lower rate than the British preference. But of course these are always in the empire.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Are these to be retroactive?
If not, are there not now certain classes of goods	in respect to which the fixed value	forduty	has been	set by	the department?	Ifthere	are such	classes	of goods, should	notthese	orders in	council	be extended and	the
goods be allowed to come in at the invoice value?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is a matter to be
considered. I am advised that the status quo will be maintained.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Under what authority is the currency dump, so-called, applied?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That does not in any
sense relate to this matter. No doubt what my hon. friend is thinking about is what is commonly called the currency dump in relation to the value of the British pound fixed for special duty purposes.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes. Under what authority
is that applied? I was under the impression that it was under this section, but apparently I am wrong. I should like to know under what authority the currency dump is applied.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There was an order in
council passed fixing the value of the pound for special duty purposes.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Under what authority was
that passed?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Under the general
authority of the statute.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Perhaps I left a wrong impression when I said that under this the dump would disappear so far as British imports are concerned, coming in under the preference. That is true only in so far as the government has power to fix artificial values with respect to prices of commodities, but I take it that the dump can still be applied if the government persists in having two valuations of the pound. Under these provisions they can still apply the dump.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, and in my answer I said, the dump in relation to 43. If there were unfair trade and an unfair value of British goods, and if it were obvious that a
special duty should be levied, we have not surrendered that right, but we have in relation to the application of section 43.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Under this item can the
minister give me any further information with regard to the dumping duty placed upon barbed wire from Holland?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The hon. member spoke to me last week with reference to the barbed wire situation. That matter has not been finally dealt with; it is under consideration. I cannot say anj'thing more at the present time.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Article 16,
which refers to this particular measure, has also this provision-

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Will my right hon.
friend allow me to interrupt him? I do not think that article 16 was framed at all with special reference to this. This is a collateral agreement.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The minister is going back to his original ground, which I think he will see is unfortunately not the right one. It is all to his credit that he should be now doing something that is in accordance with the terms of the agreement, but what I wish to ascertain is this. Article 16 provides that there will be machinery for the prompt and impartial settlement of disputes in matters pertaining to the application of tariffs. Will the minister indicate whether any machinery has been thought out or whether any exists whereby disputes in this connection may be satisfactorily adjusted? If so, what is that machinery?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not think that the suggestion with regard to machinery relates to this matter, which is very simple and does not need machinery. I would take it, however, that article 16, the part to which my right hon. friend refers, would be referred to the tariff board when set up.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Under article 16, subsection (a) provides for:
The avoidance, so far as reasonably possible, of uncertainty as to the amount of customs duties and other fiscal imposts payable on the arrival of goods in Canada.
That is to say, the government of Canada obligates to do away with these difficulties, and what the ministry is doing today is decidedly in that direction, because the minister is now depriving the government of the right to fix these high valuations, which
Customs Act

nearly always made it impossible for the importer to know in advance, or when the goods arrived, just what the amount would be- certainly an obstacle which I think it was intended to remove.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As regards the minister's statement that artiole 16 does not relate to this matter, if that be true there must be some mistake on the part of the ministry in respect to what appears in the explanatory notes attached to the bill, because these notes read:
The only change in the subsection is made by the insertion of the underlined words in the text of this bill.
The object of this amendment is to except from the operation of the section goods entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff or any lower tariff, in pursuance of the provisions of the various trade agreements concluded at the Imperial economic conference.
Now, if it is not under article 16, under which article is it?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: As I have tried to tell my right hon. friend, this is one of those trade agreements that stand upon their own feet. It was not entered into with reference to article 16.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: That raises another question.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is effecting a bilateral agreement.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The minister now tells us that there are other agreements than those before the house. What other agreements are there than those tabled?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I beg my right hon. friend's pardon. I did not say that there were other agreements besides this agreement and the trade agreement with the United Kingdom which the right hon. gentleman has been considering for weeks.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I understand that section 43 applies to goods which are imported into Canada under such conditions as prejudicially or injuriously affect the interests of Canadian producers and manufacturers. My understanding is that it is under the provisions of this section that the currency dump has been applied. If that is correct, then the currency dump will no longer apply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It will not apply to Great
Britain because this amendment exempts that country.

maintopic: CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think perhaps the minister is quite correct in his statement as to why we have this amendment to the statute now before us. The difficulty which Canadian importers of British goods were experiencing in trying to estimate the amount of duty they were going to pay, as just referred to by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), perhaps has had more to do with this amendment than the carrying out of provisions of the agreement, although, of course, that is intended as well. I am afraid my hon. friend has been learning from rather expensive experience that this is a rather poor way to enforce the tariff, and I desire to congratulate him on the introduction of this measure. I hope he will extend it and that the importer of goods into Canada will not experience the difficulty which now faces him in not knowing exactly what the amount of duty is to be until, in some cases, certain of the goods have been sold.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, November 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. 8, respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom-Mr.	Bennett-Mr.	MacDonald
(Cape Breton South) in the chair.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
The committee was considering
article 3 and schedule C.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the items covered by this article are of peculiar interest to British Columbia and one is almost justified in the conclusion that those Who participated in the preparation of this agreement were particularly keen to see to the welfare and advantage of British Columbia. This makes all the more incredible the attitude of hon. members apposite who represent constituencies in British Columbia affected by the items contained in this schedule-timber, fish, lead and zinc. We have already disposed of other items in the way of copper, fruits, apples, poultry and farm products, but I think a few concrete Statements in this connection will give an illuminating picture.
Of the first item in this schedule, timber, British Columbia produces 49 per cent of the total production in Canada; of fish, it produces 50 per cent; of lead, 98 per cent and of zinc, 90 per cent. It is about third in the dominion in the production of copper and first in the production of silver. With respect to the primary products referred to in this schedule, British Columbia holds a very enviable position.
When lumber is considered it becomes more difficult to understand the position taken by hon. members opposite from British Columbia. I refer to the hon. member for 'Skeena (Mr. Hanson), a lumberman; the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. Munn), another lumberman; the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), with large lumber interests in his constituency; the hon. taember for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), 53719-70
who comes from a district which has perhaps the largest export mill in British Columbia; and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanibury). I might mention also the other two hon. members who are interested mainly in matters affecting labour and an improved standard of living. These hon. members have opposed the agreement in toto although particularly interested in the schedule in connection with article 3. Their attitude is hard to understand when it is considered that the United Kingdom is offering the Dominion of Canada a better undertaking in connection with the purchase of lumber. Last year the total imports of lumber into the British Empire were 3,400,000,000 feet, of which Canada supplied only four per cent. British Columbia has a greater advantage than any other province in shipments of lumber to the United Kingdom, and the agreement offers to those in my province who are interested in the production of lumber the advantage of entering the United Kingdom markets absolutely free of duty as against a duty of ten per cent on lumber from foreign countries. Moreover, while the agreement specifically states ten per cent, the advantage by way of insurance, freight and so on brings the duty against lumber from other countries outside the empire to practically twenty per cent. How any member from British Columbia can, on his return to his constituents, justify his opposition to the item of lumber in schedule C, is incredible.
Let me refer now to the item of fish. We have the hon. member for Comox-Albemi and the hon. member for Skeena opposing this agreement and this schedule, and yet we find that in Skeena the production of fish last year amounted to $13,000,000 and in Comox-Alberni to $6,000,000. The United Kingdom says: We use a great quantity of fish and we are quite willing to buy British Columbia fish, and to show our good faith we are willing to permit Canadian fish to come in free of duty and to levy a tariff of ten per cent against fish from foreign countries. Last year the United Kingdom imported only $9,000,000 worth of fish from Canada and countries within the empire.
Coming next to the item of lead, we find that British Columbia produces 98 per cent of the total Canadian output, which is produced at Trail. It is good lead, being 99-99 per cent pure, and finds a market in practically every consuming country in the world, except, of course, the United States, from which it is barred by a duty of two and one-eighth cents per pound. The United Kingdom is the second largest consumer of lead in the world, and strange to say, last year it purchased from

1106	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
the United States about thirty per cent of its total import.
Then we have zinc, of which British Columbia produces ninety per cent of the total Canadian output. Last year the United Kingdom imported 157,000 tons of zinc, of which thirty per cent came from Canada and the balance from countries outside the empire. Strange to say, hon. members opposite seem to have very little realization of the great value of the production of these metals and the fact that a larger and wider market is extended to British Columbia. In this case the United Kingdom says: We are prepared to buy your lead and zinc and we are going to permit those metals to enter our market free of duty, while we impose a duty of ten per cent against similar products coming from countries outside the empire. It must also be remembered that in the case of lead and zinc, just as in that of fish and lumber, while the agreement refers to a specific duty of ten per cent against foreign lead and zinc, there is also the advantage of a duty on the insurance and freight on similar commodities from other countries.

speechtext:
May I say that nothing could better illustrate the endeavour of hon. gentlemen opposite to misrepresent those on this side of the house than the speech to which we have just listened. Over and over again the hon. member for West Kootenay said that certain members on this side had opposed this agreement because of this particular portion of it. May I say to him at once that no hon. member on this side is opposed to this particular portion. If he was, he would have so stated long before the imperial conference ever took place because these British duties according a preference to the dominion were not put on at the recent imperial conference but were put on by the British government many months before the conference ever took place. This schedule relates to timber, fish, salmon, other fish, canned, asbestos, zinc and lead, and on 53719-701
every one of these particular articles mentioned the British government at the time it introduced its tariff gave a ten per cent preference to the dominions, and the rate which is given under this agreement is ten per cent. So the British government have simply continued the same rate of preference. Is it conceivable that at the recent conference the government of Canada would have asked Great Britain to do away with the preference which she had given months before the conference was ever held? What we are opposing in so far as it touches this matter at all are the representations of hon. gentlemen opposite that what has been secured in the treaty in this particular is due to some effort of theirs. It is not due to some effort of theirs. It is just another example of the same thing that took place this afternoon in connection with the bill the Minister of National Revenue was concerned with. We have to thank the British government, not our own government, for what there is of advantage to Canada in this part of the agreement, because what is here set forth was granted before our own government had anything to do with the conference at all.
May I add a further point? Probably hon. members will say: Oh yes, but we have persuaded Great Britain to keep these preferences on, and to remove them only upon the consent of the government of Canada. On Friday evening I touched on that feature. In so far as that contention has any significance at all it constitutes interference by one government with the affairs of another, and similar interference at the instance of the British parliament or government we would not stand for for one minute. If in Great Britain they wish to make their agreements subject to conditions of that kind it is their own business, but it is not a precedent that we are going to follow. May I add that the Secretary of the Treasury in Great Britain made a specific statement in the British house that so far as the British parliament was concerned, it would not regard itself bound by these duties any longer than the parliament of Great Britain wished to have themselves so bound. Over and over again it has been slated by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this house that the British government is perfectly free to change these duties at any time they like except in so far as they may regard themselves as in honour bound. But they are not in any way legally or constitutionally bound.

I am quite certain that
the right hon. gentleman does not mean to misinterpret or misrepresent my statement, but he has not stated it quite clearly. maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM

What we are criticizing in this particular schedule is not what the hon. member for West Kootenay would have the house and the country believe, a preference being continued which was granted to us by the British government before the conference took place, but rather the representations of gentlemen like himself who would seek to have the country believe that this is something which the Canadian government were responsible for bringing about at the recent conference and that we should be thankful at this moment for having this particular preference because of the Canadian government's efforts. The right hon. gentleman is beating about the bush. These agreements go into force tomorrow in the United Kingdom, and lead and zinc from the empire will continue to enter the United Kingdom free *of duty. Surely the imposition of a tariff against lead and zinc from non-empire countries was a part of the conference agreement. We all admit that empire lead goes into the United Kingdom at world prices, but lead from outside the empire does not, and must pay a duty of ten per cent. If that is not a satisfactory result from the conference, it is pretty hard to tell what could be. W'hen the right hon. gentleman opposite charges that we stress these particular items Under schedule C, I say we have good cause to do so. Schedule C is part of the agreement. They have recorded their opposition to the benefits contained in schedule C by refusing to ratify the agreement. In other words they have said: "We do not want our Canadian copper to enter the United Kingdom market enjoying a preference of four cents per pound against other copper; we do not want our lead or zinc to enter the United Kingdom free. We do not wish our fish or our lumber to enjoy advantages in the British market." Hon. members opposite do not want anything that would increase or encourage production or industry in the Dominion of Canada. That is the situation.

speechtext:
It would seem that hon. members opposite do not realize that during the debate on the Dunning budget of 1930 the then leader of the opposition stated the gov-vernment of the day was stealing the policy of the Conservative party, and stated further his opposition to a British preference.
Now, so far as northern Ontario and our consideration of trade policies is concerned, our policy has always been that first of all we should patronize Canadian industry and buy Canadian goods; secondly that we should buy goods within the British Empire, and thirdly those from foreign countries. I wish to say this, before I am through, that in northern Ontario we need not only the British market, but also the markets of the world. There is one statement to which I wish to make reference before I proceed further. Speaking last Thursday the Prime Minister made a statement which in my view reflects upon the house. At that time he wished to create the impression throughout the width and breadth of the country that the present session of parliament is costing an enormous sum of money. That is not a true statement of the facts. First of all we all know that we came here under the unwritten understanding that we would receive no more money than we would get at an ordinary session. And, secondly, I am sure that the country would not for one moment begrudge the money paid the sessional employees in and around the parliament buildings. If, as the Prime Minister states it will cost the country $100,000, in my view the expenditure is warranted. He must realize that some of the people engaged in the house will be out of employment from the adjournment until the sittings are resumed after the New Year. I notice the hon. member for Argenteuil is laughing. However it is not a laughing matter for a lot of people who must earn their bread and butter from the present session.
At this time I should like to place before the house and country as forcibly as possible the situation which obtains in northern Ontario. I am not a sob-sister artist, but I shall endeavour to outline the facts as they exist. First of all I shall deal with the present situation, and secondly I shall deal with the needs of industry. I believe I am in order when I direct my attention to these matters, and that my remarks may come under schedule
C of the agreement. First of all, I stated on every possible occasion since the last general election campaign that if hon. members opposite took office we would have no longer an export market in the United States for pulpwood produced in northern Canada. This statement applies not only to the wooded areas of northern Ontario but to the whole of northern Canada.
During the last election campaign I protested vigorously against statements made by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) and by some ministers of the Ontario government, that we should be restricted from exporting pulpwood into the United States. In a few brief moments I shall show, Mr. Chairman, that the only market we have for our surplus pulpwood is in the United States. Following the principles laid down by the Prime Minister we could not sell that pulpwood to the United States market.
In the province of Ontario-and I believe the same system is followed in the whole of Canada-primarily the land belongs to the crown. In enticing industries to come to the northern section of the province there were granted to those industries some large areas of timber lands. Some of the lands so granted were to the extent of 5,000 square miles, and I believe that at that time such grants were justified. Industries investing about $100,000,000 in the northern country should have been given a permanent supply of raw material, so far as newsprint is concerned. Then, secondly, there is the land which belongs to the crown, and from which land the government has nevei taken pulpwood. Then, thirdly, there is the freeholder, the man who a few years ago took holdings in northern Ontario, eventually receiving a deed from the government. The deed he received gave him full rights with the exception of mineral rights, to any resources found on the farm. It is also a fact that the Ontario government has parcelled out several sections of northern Ontario to private interests, and such interests are primarily interested in cutting timber and pulpwood for exportation to the United States.
I said a few minutes ago that the big newsprint interests have their own limits, so that we would expect first of all they would cut from those lands. For fifty miles on each side of their limits however they buy from the settlers but those living further away naturally must necessarily find a market for their pulpwood. Again I say that the American market is the only place in which we can satisfactorily dispose of any pulpwood surplus we may have in any section of Canada. We will recall a time during the session of 1931 when the present Prime Minister stated that

foreign countries have to buy raw materials from Canada. This is a statement which will not stand investigation, because we find that at. the next session a restriction was placed upon the export of pulpwood from Canada to the United States. That country was forced to buy most of its pulpwood from Russia. In the pulpwood industry there is competition from the Scandinavian countries, and, in a small measure from Germany. Those countries were in a position largely to supply the pulpwood requirements of the United States. I should like hon. members to realize that the pulpwood exported from northern Ontario is as far as the settler is concerned, a finished product, the same as wheat is said to be the finished product of the western farmer. He sells his wheat in its original form. When the domestic market has been saturated he must look to an outside market. That outside market, so far as pulpwood is concerned, cannot be found within the British Empire. Certainly, it has to be found within the United States, because if hon. members would consult the quarterly reports of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the years 1929, 1930, 1931 and 1932 they would find that not a single stick of pulpwood was shipped to any point within the empire outside of Canada.
I should like to read to the house some figures so that hon. members may realize the timber situation in Canada. The only market we have at the present time is the one that we have tried to shut off. It may be all very well to cut out unfair competition in manufactured products, but what are we to do with our pulpwood when in northern Ontario we have a big surplus. As I said a few moments ago, not a single cord of pulpwood finds its way to any country within the British Empire; all our pulpwood is sold in the United States.
